transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-17
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood SE), Michael Torres (Aurora CTO), Sara Nguyen (Aurora Head of Security), Liam Patel (Aurora Sr Eng)

Summary (auto): Short demo focused on retention controls, logging redaction, PII handling and request storage toggles in Redwood Console + API. Customer wants clear auditability and ability to opt-out of storing request payloads for regulated transactions.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex from Redwood, this is Priya and Jordan. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Michael Torres: Good, thanks. Busy quarter but excited to see this — Sara's got a few security questions.
[00:12] Sara Nguyen: Yep, hi all. Main things for us: where are logs stored, can we redact fields automatically, does the request store include PII by default, and how do you integrate with our KMS?
[00:22] Priya Kapoor: Great, we'll walk through the console first and then show API toggles. Quick note—I might mumble product names, sometimes the recorder shows "Redwood Inferns" or something :-)
[00:30] Jordan Li: We'll aim to demo three things: configurable retention windows per-route, logging redaction rules (regexp and schema-based), and the request storage toggle that can prevent payloads from being persisted.
[00:40] Liam Patel: When you say per-route, do you mean per-endpoint or per-model?
[00:44] Priya Kapoor: Both. You can set retention at route level in the console, which maps to API routes; you can also pin model variants and have separate policies. For example you can set payments endpoints to zero-day retention while dev endpoints keep 90 days.
[00:56] Michael Torres: Zero-day means no storage at all? Do you still keep audit metadata?
[01:01] Priya Kapoor: Good question. We differentiate between request payload storage and metadata/audit logs. If you enable "no request storage" for a route, request and response bodies are not persisted — only minimal metadata like timestamp, route id, and outcome codes are stored for operational purposes, and you can choose to truncate or drop even that. We'll show the toggle.
[01:18] Sara Nguyen: And that metadata is encrypted with our KMS?
[01:21] Priya Kapoor: Yes, Redwood supports customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for encryption at rest. You can configure key rotation policies from your cloud KMS, and logs are encrypted using that key. We also support envelope encryption for extra protection.
[01:33] Michael Torres: Do you allow field-level redaction? For example, a card number field in a prompt — can that be stripped before persistence?
[01:39] Priya Kapoor: Absolutely. We have two redaction paths: automatic regex-based redaction you can apply globally or per-route, and schema-aware redactors where you upload a JSON schema and mark fields as sensitive. The schema approach is more robust for structured payloads.
[01:52] Liam Patel: How reliable is the schema redaction for noisy prompts? We send some user messages that include free text which may include PII in sentence form.
[01:58] Jordan Li: For free text we recommend a hybrid approach: use regex patterns for common PII shapes (SSN, card numbers, email) and then run an optional on-the-fly classifier that marks tokens before they're written. Note that classifier inference can be done locally in the private deployment for extra guarantees.
[02:14] Michael Torres: Is that classifier part of Redwood or do we bring our own?
[02:18] Priya Kapoor: Redwood provides a built-in classifier, but you can also supply a custom function or lambda in the request pipeline that returns redaction masks. It's exposed in both hosted and private deployments, but for high-security setups customers often run the classifier in their VPC so nothing leaves their network.
[02:33] Sara Nguyen: We need a paper trail — full audit logs for compliance. If a retention is set to zero, do we still keep who changed the policy and when?
[02:41] Alex Chen: Yes, audit trails for admin actions are kept separately — you can configure retention for those logs; for compliance you can export them to your SIEM (Splunk/Datadog) or to an S3 bucket under your account for long-term retention. Admin audit logs include actor, timestamp, ip, and the change diff.
[02:58] Michael Torres: Can you show the console now?
[03:00] Priya Kapoor: Sure — switching screens. (brief pause) Sorry, the recorder sometimes shows our app as "Redwood Optima" in the transcript, ignore that.
[03:12] [screen share audio] Priya Kapoor: Here's the console route list. I'll open the payments-route config. On the right you'll see retention, redaction, and request-storage toggles.
[03:23] [00:03] Priya Kapoor: First toggle is 'Persist request payloads' — enabled by default. If I flip it off, you get a confirmation modal that explains that responses won't be available for debugging. There's also a per-environment override so you can keep dev logs and disable prod storage.
[03:40] Liam Patel: Is that toggle available via API? We want to automate it per-customer.
[03:44] Jordan Li: Yes — we have an API endpoint: PATCH /v1/routes/{route_id}/policy with body fields retention_days, persist_requests (true/false), redaction_rules. We'll send the snippet after the call.
[03:56] Michael Torres: When persist_requests is false, is there any chance the downstream model provider receives data? I mean, the model still processes the text — but does Redwood store it anywhere transiently?
[04:06] Priya Kapoor: The model processing happens in-memory on the serving tier. By default, we do not persist request/response content to disk when persist_requests is false. However some transient buffers may exist in process memory until the request completes. For extra assurance we offer a private deployment option where the entire control plane and data plane stay in your VPC so nothing is sent to Redwood hosted storage.
[04:24] Sara Nguyen: Does the auditing for canary or debug traces include sample outputs? We need to ensure debug traces are anonymized.
[04:30] Priya Kapoor: Debug traces are a separate setting. You can enable 'trace mode' for a session and set it so traces are redacted automatically. We also have a scrubber pipeline that can be applied to any trace export to strip PII before it's delivered to a third-party system.
[04:45] Michael Torres: Is there a possibility of false positives with regex redaction removing legitimate non-PII tokens? Could break debugging.
[04:51] Jordan Li: Yes that's why we recommend a test harness — Redwood Optimize includes a preflight eval where you run a corpus and get redaction impact metrics showing false positives/negatives so you can tune rules before turning them on in prod.
[05:05] Liam Patel: Ok, about encryption in transit — you support mutual TLS?
[05:09] Alex Chen: We support mTLS for Dedicated and Private deployments. For hosted API, we use TLS with client certs optional — we can do mTLS on request if you require it via a customer endpoint.
[05:19] Sara Nguyen: How is role-based access handled for retention settings? We don't want devs to flip retention accidentally.
[05:24] Priya Kapoor: RBAC is built into the Console. You can restrict Route policy edits to admins only. There's also an approval workflow: changes to retention or persist_requests can require an approval from a compliance AD group before they get applied. We integrate with SSO/SAML and SCIM to sync groups.
[05:41] Michael Torres: Great. Can you show an example audit export?
[05:44] Priya Kapoor: Sure — exporting. (pause) Here's an export preview. You can see event_type, actor, timestamp, route_id, policy_before, policy_after. The policy diffs are JSON but if you prefer we can send them in CSV for ingestion.
[06:00] Sara Nguyen: One more on keys — do you support bringing your own key (BYOK) and HSM-backed keys?
[06:06] Jordan Li: Yes BYOK via AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or an HSM integration. Keys are used to encrypt persisted data at rest and can be rotated. We support split-key or envelope encryption patterns for higher assurance.
[06:18] Michael Torres: Performance impact — if we enable schema redaction and classifier, what's the added latency?
[06:24] Priya Kapoor: In hosted mode, regex redaction is negligible (<5ms). Schema redaction and local classifier can add 10-40ms depending on model and runtime; if you run the classifier in private deployment inside your VPC it's typically sub-20ms. We can run a benchmark during POC.
[06:38] Liam Patel: For PII detection, can we write a custom function that returns a mask so we never send masked tokens to the model?
[06:45] Priya Kapoor: Yes — you can hook a preprocessor lambda that returns a masked prompt. In Dedicated and Private setups customers often pre-process to remove PII and send a tokenized delta to the model.
[06:58] Michael Torres: About compliance: can we set different retention windows per customer segment? We have enterprise customers that require 7 years retention for audit, but for EU customers we might want data residency.
[07:08] Priya Kapoor: That's supported. You can attach policies by tag: region, customer-tier, route, or model. For data residency, Redwood Dedicated/Private can keep data in your cloud region or on-prem. For hosted customers we have region-specific controls and can pin storage to EU regions for GDPR.
[07:24] Sara Nguyen: Do you provide data deletion APIs (right to be forgotten)?
[07:27] Jordan Li: Yes — delete endpoints let you expunge request content by id or by selector (time range, route, customer id). Deletion will scrub bodies and optionally scrub the corresponding n-gram caches as well. There is also a certificate-backed purge for compliance audits.
[07:40] Michael Torres: N-gram cache — does Redwood persist any model caches that might leak content?
[07:45] Priya Kapoor: We persist KV caches for generation acceleration, but those caches don't include full prompts; they include key/value activations. For super-sensitive pipelines we have an option to disable persistent KV caching or to shard caches per-tenant with immediate eviction on request.
[08:00] Liam Patel: Can you show the API snippet for toggling persist_requests?
[08:03] Jordan Li: Sure, I'll paste it in chat after. Quick demo: PATCH /v1/routes/payments-prod/policy body { "retention_days": 0, "persist_requests": false, "redaction_rules": [ { "type": "regex", "pattern": "\\b\\d{4}-\\d{4}-\\d{4}-\\d{4}\\b", "action": "mask" } ] }
[08:28] Michael Torres: Thanks. Could you also show the sample logs we would export to our S3? I want to verify fields.
[08:33] Priya Kapoor: Export contains event_time, route_id, actor, action, outcome_code, resource_id, and a payload_digest if you keep payloads. If you set persist_requests false, payload_digest will be null.
[08:46] Sara Nguyen: What about developer troubleshooting — will turning off storage make debugging impossible?
[08:50] Priya Kapoor: It makes post-hoc debugging harder, yes. We suggest using short-term retention windows (e.g., 7 days) for production plus a strict redaction pipeline, or enabling ephemeral debug traces that are gated by approval and auto-expire.
[09:03] Michael Torres: Any network egress concerns for hosted customers? We need to show legal that no PII is routed to third parties.
[09:10] Alex Chen: For hosted customers, Redwood is the data processor — we publish subprocessors and you can request data flow diagrams. For Private deployments, that's on-prem and you control egress. We also support contractual clauses (DPA) to restrict subprocessors.
[09:23] Sara Nguyen: Competitors question — How is this different from OpenAI's retention settings?
[09:27] Alex Chen: OpenAI has some retention controls but Redwood focuses on per-route policies, BYOK, and deeper console tooling (Audit flows, approval gates, and redaction harness integrated with Redwood Optimize). We also provide Dedicated/Private deployments that keep the entire runtime in-customer.
[09:42] Michael Torres: Ok excellent. Let's talk POC scope — we want to validate: 1) retention toggle works and prevents persistence 2) redaction rules catch PII in free text with acceptable FP rate 3) KMS integration and audit export to S3
[09:56] Alex Chen: Sounds good — proposed POC steps: provision a sandbox Dedicated instance or Private trial in your AWS account; ingest a sample corpus; run Redwood Optimize redaction preflight; run throughput and latency benchmarks; produce audit export to your S3.
[10:10] Liam Patel: Timeline? We need this before month end.
[10:13] Alex Chen: We can aim to start 2026-11-24 and run a 2-week POC. Priya will coordinate.
[10:19] Sara Nguyen: Security review — can you send the SOC2 / ISO attestation and a network diagram?
[10:24] Alex Chen: We'll send the security whitepaper and an architecture diagram with subprocessors. Also will include the contractual DPA.
[10:31] Michael Torres: Awesome. Any last quick clarifications?
[10:34] Priya Kapoor: One quick note on billing: disabling request storage doesn't change inference per-token billing; it's purely storage/retention controls. There may be small additional charges for KMS operations depending on cloud provider.
[10:46] Michael Torres: Makes sense.
[10:47] Alex Chen: Ok recap — we'll: 1) send SOC2/security whitepaper + KMS docs, 2) share API snippets and console screenshots, 3) schedule POC for the week of 11/24, 4) provide trial credentials for Dedicated evaluation, 5) Priya will run a redaction preflight on a sample corpus once Michael confirms dataset.
[11:05] Jordan Li: I'll paste the PATCH snippet + retention examples into the chat now and upload the demo deck to the shared drive.
[11:12] Michael Torres: Thanks — Sara will follow up with a list of compliance items.
[11:16] Sara Nguyen: Thanks everyone.
[11:18] Alex Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up via email.

Notes on transcription quirks: occasional mis-heard names, product names appear as "Redwood Optima" or "Redwood Inferns" in the auto-summary. Regex patterns in transcript may show double-escaping due to recorder.
